lesson.title: When the Experimental Unit Is a Person: Understanding Subjects
lesson.summary: Subjects are the human experimental units in a study, a distinction that matters because people can think, have expectations, and react to being studied in ways that plots of land or machines cannot.
lesson.body:
When the experimental units in a study are people, statisticians call them subjects rather than just units. The word signals that something beyond the mechanics of assigning a treatment and measuring a response is now in play, because human subjects can think, have expectations, and react to the mere fact of being studied, none of which is true of a plot of farmland.

Because subjects are people, experiments involving them carry ethical obligations that experiments on plots or machines do not. Researchers must obtain informed consent, meaning subjects agree to participate after being told what the study involves and what risks it carries, subjects must be free to withdraw at any point without penalty, and studies must typically be reviewed by an ethics board before they begin. None of these requirements apply to a plot of farmland or a batch of manufactured parts, which is exactly why the vocabulary shift from experimental unit to subject matters, it flags that a different set of rules now governs the study. Subjects also introduce a purely psychological complication: a person who knows they are receiving a new treatment, or who simply knows they are being watched, may change their behavior or genuinely feel different as a result of that knowledge alone, independent of whether the treatment does anything physiologically. This is the seed of an idea, the placebo effect, that later sections examine in detail.

Suppose a researcher recruits 100 volunteers with chronic headaches for a pain-relief drug trial. Those 100 volunteers are the subjects, the human experimental units, of the study. If the researcher randomly assigns 50 subjects to receive the new drug and 50 to receive a sugar pill, and the drug group reports an average pain reduction of 3.2 points on a 10 point scale while the sugar pill group reports a reduction of 1.1 points, the comparison is only trustworthy if both groups of subjects were treated identically in every way except the pill's actual chemical content, including not knowing which pill they received, since a subject's belief about the treatment can itself shape the outcome.

This is why studies with human subjects frequently go further than experiments on inanimate units, using techniques such as blinding subjects to which treatment they received and comparing against a control group that receives a placebo, an inactive treatment that looks identical to the real one. These tools exist specifically because subjects are experimental units capable of reacting to expectation, not just to the treatment itself.

Recognizing when your experimental units are subjects, rather than plots, tires, or petri dishes, is not just a vocabulary exercise. It flags exactly which additional design safeguards, informed consent, blinding, placebo comparison, a study needs before its results can be believed.
